summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the full United States federal framework applies on the island: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework; in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be subject to hand search. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment and prosthetics may be carried through the checkpoint after screening. The National Center for Transgender Equality publishes packing guidance intended to reduce the risk of invasive searches; that federal procedure applies at Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport and at other airports serving Puerto Rico.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21 and barred public funding for it. Doctors who violate the ban face up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of their licences. The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so that physicians and affirming parents who facilitate hormone therapy or top surgery risk prosecution. It also mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the supposed risks of trans-affirming care. The Health Secretary, Carlos Ramos Otero, proposed amendments that would have permitted puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone therapy; the enacted text did not adopt them. A 2025 report describes it as the most extreme restriction on trans medical care in any United States jurisdiction, and the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation has announced plans to challenge it in court.

Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico. Executive Order 14168 directs federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The American Civil Liberties Union said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people in its custody. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that a transgender inmate's housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or judicial ruling was located.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. Enforcement is recent and its record thin: 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged on Bonilla's confession that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage for a visitor is narrow. The 2013 law that did pass, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House so that it applies only to employment discrimination, leaving public facilities, housing, business transactions and public transportation uncovered. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation across those settings, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.
tangentialFactors:
The route to relationship recognition in Puerto Rico ran through federal court rather than the territorial legislature. The Ada Conde Vidal case, filed in March 2014, drew in four additional same-sex couples that June, represented by Lambda Legal with PR Para Todas intervening; one couple had married in Canada in 2007 and another in New York in 2012, and among the plaintiffs was a former National Guard member.

Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002. After the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas decision in 2003 struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

Legislative attempts to weaken protections have a record of failing. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 pairing, SB1253 and SB1254, was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests; the conversion-therapy ban in that pairing carried a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy.
localsOnly:
The territorial anti-discrimination statute protects only in employment, a limitation that binds residents as well as visitors and leaves LGBTQ people without statutory recourse for refusal of service, housing or access to public facilities. Public facilities remain uncovered because of the 2013 House amendment to Senate Bill 238.

Conversion therapy for minors remains legal in Puerto Rico. A ban, SB1000, died in the House in March 2019 when the pro-statehood NPP caucus blocked a floor vote despite Senate passage and the governor's support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, publicly dissented.

The 2019 religious freedom pairing drew sustained opposition from LGBT advocates. In April 2019 Governor Rosselló had announced SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, alongside SB1254, a conversion therapy ban with a pastoral exemption; the LGBT council president, Johanne Velez Garcia, and allied organisations said the pair would open doors to discrimination, arguing that the religious-freedom carve-out would license refusal of service on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills in June 2019.

House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The care ban's practical effect on residents is compounded by its mandate that the Education and Health departments run public campaigns about the risks of trans-affirming care, and by the prosecutions it authorises against parents as well as physicians.
outOfScopeNotes:
The enforcement record for Puerto Rico's July 2025 care ban is not yet sourced. No prosecutions, regulatory actions or court rulings applying it were located, and no report of its application to adult non-residents seeking care on the island was found.

The outcome of the criminal cases arising from the 22 April 2020 murders of two transgender women is not sourced here; the inventory establishes the charges and the confession, not the verdict or sentence.

The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the care ban in court, but no filing date, court or docket was located.

No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or judicial ruling was located, so the conditions of trans people in territorial custody, as distinct from federal custody, remain unresolved.

Whether the January 2025 state of emergency over violence against transgender individuals produced funded programmes or an operative protection mechanism is not sourced.
